courses.title: UI/UX Design Fundamentals
courses.description: Learn the fundamentals of UI/UX design including user research, wireframing, prototyping, and usability testing.

lessons.title: What is UI/UX Design?
lessons.body:
UI (User Interface) focuses on the visual elements of a product — buttons, layouts, colors, and typography. UX (User Experience) is about how the product feels — the flow, accessibility, and satisfaction of using it. Together, they create products that are both beautiful and functional.

In this course, we'll cover the complete design process from research to high-fidelity prototypes.

lessons.title: User Research Methods
lessons.body:
Understanding your users is the foundation of great design. Key research methods include:

- **Interviews**: One-on-one conversations to understand user needs and pain points
- **Surveys**: Quantitative data from larger groups
- **Observation**: Watching users interact with existing products
- **Personas**: Fictional characters representing your target users
- **Journey Maps**: Visualizing the user's experience over time

The goal is to build empathy and identify real problems to solve.

lessons.title: Wireframing Basics
lessons.body:
Wireframes are low-fidelity sketches of your interface. They focus on structure and layout, not visual design.

Key principles:
- Start with pen and paper for quick iteration
- Use gray boxes for content placeholders
- Focus on information hierarchy
- Keep it simple — no colors, fonts, or images yet
- Annotate interactions and edge cases

Tools: Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD, or even paper and pencil.

lessons.title: Color Theory for Interfaces
lessons.body:
Color is one of the most powerful tools in a designer's toolkit. It communicates hierarchy, status, brand identity, and emotion.

The 60-30-10 Rule:
- 60% dominant color (background)
- 30% secondary color (cards, sections)
- 10% accent color (buttons, CTAs)

Accessibility matters: Always ensure sufficient contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text). Use tools like WebAIM Contrast Checker.

lessons.title: Typography Fundamentals
lessons.body:
Typography makes or breaks a design. Good typography guides the eye, creates hierarchy, and sets the tone.

Key concepts:
- **Font pairing**: Use 2 fonts max (one for headings, one for body)
- **Scale**: Use a modular scale (e.g., 1.25x) for consistent sizing
- **Line height**: 1.4–1.6 for body text
- **Line length**: 50–75 characters per line is optimal
- **Weight**: Use weight (bold/regular) for hierarchy, not size alone

Recommended Google Fonts: Inter, Outfit, DM Sans, Plus Jakarta Sans.

lessons.title: Prototyping with Figma
lessons.body:
Prototypes bring your designs to life before writing any code. They let you test interactions and gather feedback early.

Figma Prototype Features:
- **Frames**: Artboards for each screen state
- **Interactions**: Click, hover, and drag triggers
- **Animations**: Smart animate for smooth transitions
- **Components**: Reusable UI elements with variants
- **Prototype links**: Connect frames to simulate navigation

Start with low-fidelity click-through prototypes, then refine with animations.

lessons.title: Usability Testing
lessons.body:
Usability testing is watching real users try to complete tasks with your design. It's the fastest way to find problems.

How to run a test:
1. Define 3–5 key tasks to test
recruit 5 users (5 tests find ~85% of issues)
3. Give minimal instruction — let them figure it out
4. Think aloud: Ask them to narrate their thoughts
5. Observe, don't help
6. Take notes on where they struggle

Tools: Maze, UserTesting, Hotjar, or even Zoom + screen share.

lessons.title: Design Systems
lessons.body:
A design system is a collection of reusable components, patterns, and guidelines that ensure consistency across a product.

Essential components:
- **Design tokens**: Colors, spacing, typography variables
- **Component library**: Buttons, inputs, cards, modals
- **Pattern library**: Form layouts, navigation, empty states
- **Documentation**: Usage guidelines and examples

Why build one? It speeds up design, ensures consistency, and makes collaboration easier. Start small and grow organically.

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.body:
Responsive design ensures your interface works on any screen size. With mobile traffic exceeding desktop, this is non-negotiable.

Approaches:
- **Mobile-first**: Design for mobile, then scale up
- **Breakpoints**: Common breakpoints at 480px, 768px, 1024px, 1280px
- **Flexible grids**: Use CSS Grid or Flexbox with relative units
- **Fluid typography**: Use clamp() for responsive font sizes
- **Touch targets**: Minimum 44x44px for tap targets

Test on real devices, not just browser resize.

lessons.title: Handoff to Developers
lessons.body:
The design-to-dev handoff is where great designs either succeed or fail. Clear communication is key.

What to include:
- **Specs**: Exact sizes, spacing, and colors
- **Assets**: Exported icons, images, and SVGs
- **Interactions**: Documented behavior for each component
- **Edge cases**: Empty states, errors, loading states
- **Responsive behavior**: How layouts adapt

Figma's Dev Mode makes this seamless. Annotate your designs and use auto-layout for spacing accuracy.

lessons.title: Portfolio Best Practices
lessons.body:
Your portfolio is your most important career asset. It should showcase your process, not just final screens.

Structure each case study as:
1. **Problem**: What challenge did you solve?
2. **Process**: How did you approach it? (Research → Ideation → Design → Test)
3. **Solution**: Show your designs with context
4. **Impact**: What were the results? (Metrics, feedback)

Tips:
- Show 3–5 of your best projects
- Include failed experiments (shows growth mindset)
- Write clearly — designers are communicators
- Keep it updated with your latest work

lessons.title: Final Project: Design a Mobile App
lessons.body:
Put everything you've learned into practice. Design a complete mobile app from concept to high-fidelity prototype.

Your deliverables:
1. User persona and journey map
2. Low-fidelity wireframes (5+ screens)
3. Mood board and style guide
4. High-fidelity mockups
5. Interactive prototype in Figma
6. Brief case study documenting your process

Choose a real problem you care about. The best portfolios tell stories of meaningful work. Good luck!

courses.title: React - Complete Guide
courses.description: Master React from basics to advanced concepts including hooks, context, performance optimization, and testing.

lessons.title: Introduction to React
lessons.body:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, created by Meta. It uses a component-based architecture where you build encapsulated components that manage their own state.

Why React?
- Declarative: Describe what the UI should look like
- Component-based: Build encapsulated, reusable pieces
- Learn once, write anywhere: React Native for mobile
- Huge ecosystem: Libraries for everything

Setup: Create a new app with `npx create-react-app my-app` or use Vite for faster builds.

lessons.title: JSX and Components
lessons.body:
JSX is a syntax extension that looks like HTML but compiles to JavaScript function calls. ```jsx function Greeting({ name }) { return

Hello, {name}!

; } ``` Key rules: - JSX must return a single root element (use fragments `<>...` for multiple) - Use `className` instead of `class` - JavaScript expressions in curly braces `{}` - Components must be PascalCase - Always close self-closing tags (``)

lessons.title: Props and State
lessons.body:
**Props** are read-only data passed from parent to child:
```jsx
<Greeting name="Alice" age={25} />
```

**State** is mutable data managed within a component:
```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```

Golden rules:
- Never modify props directly
- State updates trigger re-renders
- State should be lifted up when siblings need it
- Use the functional form of setState when new state depends on old: `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`

lessons.title: useEffect and Side Effects
lessons.body:
`useEffect` lets you perform side effects in functional components:

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
  return () => cleanup(); // cleanup function
}, [count]); // dependency array
```

Dependency array behavior:
- No array: Runs after every render
- Empty array `[]`: Runs once on mount
- With deps `[a, b]`: Runs when a or b change

Common patterns:
- Data fetching
- Subscriptions (WebSocket, event listeners)
- DOM manipulation
- Timer management

lessons.title: Handling Events and Forms
lessons.body:
Event handling in React uses camelCase naming:

```jsx
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
<input onChange={handleChange} value={text} />
```

Form handling patterns:
- **Controlled components**: React state drives form values
- **Uncontrolled components**: DOM manages form values (useRef)
- **Form validation**: Validate on submit, show errors inline

For complex forms, consider libraries like React Hook Form for better performance and DX.

lessons.title: React Router
lessons.body:
React Router enables navigation in single-page applications:

```jsx
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link } from 'react-router-dom';

<BrowserRouter>
  <nav><Link to="/">Home</Link></nav>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>
```

Key concepts:
- `<Routes>` and `<Route>` define your route tree
- `useParams()` to access URL parameters
- `useNavigate()` for programmatic navigation
- `useSearchParams()` for query strings
- Nested routes with `<Outlet />`

courses.title: Python for Beginners
courses.description: Complete Python course covering basics, OOP, data structures, file handling, and real-world projects.

lessons.title: Getting Started with Python
lessons.body:
Python is a high-level, interpreted language known for its readability and versatility. It's used in web development, data science, AI, automation, and more.

Setup:
1. Install Python from python.org
2. Use VS Code with the Python extension
3. Run your first script: `print('Hello, World!')`

Python uses indentation (4 spaces) for code blocks instead of braces. This enforces clean, readable code.

lessons.title: Variables and Data Types
lessons.body:
Python is dynamically typed — you don't declare variable types:

```python
name = "Alice"       # str
age = 25              # int
gpa = 3.9             # float
is_student = True     # bool
```

Key operations:
- String formatting: `f"Hello, {name}!"`
- Type checking: `type(variable)`
- Type conversion: `int("42")`, `str(42)`
- f-strings are preferred over `.format()` or `%`

lessons.title: Control Flow
lessons.body:
Conditionals:
```python
if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
else:
    grade = "C"
```

Loops:
```python
for i in range(5):     # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
    print(i)

while x > 0:
    x -= 1
```

Useful patterns:
- `enumerate()` for index + value
- `zip()` for parallel iteration
- List comprehensions: `[x**2 for x in range(10)]`

lessons.title: Lists and Dictionaries
lessons.body:
**Lists** (ordered, mutable):
```python
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("date")
fruits[0]  # "apple"
```

**Dictionaries** (key-value pairs):
```python
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}
person["name"]  # "Alice"
person.get("email", "N/A")  # default value
```

**Tuples** (ordered, immutable):
```python
point = (3, 4)
```

**Sets** (unique values):
```python
unique = {1, 2, 3, 2}  # {1, 2, 3}
```

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.body:
Functions encapsulate reusable logic:

```python
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    """Greet someone."""
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"
```

Key concepts:
- Default parameters (must come last)
- `*args` and `**kwargs` for flexible arguments
- Lambda functions: `square = lambda x: x**2`
- Docstrings for documentation
- Type hints: `def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:`

Higher-order functions:
- `map()`, `filter()`, `sorted()` with key functions

lessons.title: Object-Oriented Programming
lessons.body:
OOP organizes code into classes and objects:

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.name = name
        self.breed = breed

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

my_dog = Dog("Rex", "Labrador")
```

Key concepts:
- **Encapsulation**: Bundle data and methods together
- **Inheritance**: `class Puppy(Dog):`
- **Polymorphism**: Same method, different behavior
- **Magic methods**: `__str__`, `__len__`, `__eq__`

lessons.title: File Handling
lessons.body:
Python makes file I/O straightforward:

```python
# Reading
with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()

# Writing
with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello, World!")

# CSV
import csv
with open("data.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row["name"])
```

Always use `with` statements — they handle file closing automatically.

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.body:
Graceful error handling prevents crashes:

```python
try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Unexpected: {e}")
else:
    print("No errors")
finally:
    print("Always runs")
```

Best practices:
- Catch specific exceptions, not broad `Exception`
- Use custom exceptions for your domain
- Log errors, don't silently ignore them
- EAFP: Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission

courses.title: Data Science with R
courses.description: Learn data science with R including data visualization, statistical analysis, and machine learning basics.

lessons.title: Introduction to R
lessons.body:
R is a language and environment designed for statistical computing and graphics. It's widely used in academia and industry for data analysis.

Why R?
- Powerful statistical capabilities
- Excellent visualization with ggplot2
- Rich ecosystem of packages (CRAN)
- RStudio provides a fantastic IDE
- Strong community support

Install R and RStudio, then try: `print('Hello, Data!')`

lessons.title: Data Structures in R
lessons.body:
R's core data structures:

- **Vectors**: `x <- c(1, 2, 3)` — the basic building block
- **Matrices**: `m <- matrix(1:9, nrow=3)` — 2D numeric data
- **Lists**: `l <- list(name="Alice", age=25)` — mixed types
- **Data Frames**: `df <- data.frame(x=1:3, y=c("a","b","c"))` — the workhorse

Data frames are like spreadsheets in code. Each column is a vector, and columns can have different types.

lessons.title: Data Manipulation with dplyr
lessons.body:
dplyr is the go-to package for data manipulation:

```r
library(dplyr)

df %>%
  filter(age > 25) %>%          # rows
  select(name, score) %>%        # columns
  mutate(grade = score / 10) %>% # new columns
  arrange(desc(score)) %>%       # sorting
  group_by(category) %>%         # grouping
  summarize(avg = mean(score))   # aggregation
```

The pipe operator `%>%` chains operations left-to-right, making code readable.

lessons.title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
lessons.body:
ggplot2 implements the Grammar of Graphics for building plots layer by layer:

```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(x = age, y = score, color = category)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Score vs Age", x = "Age", y = "Score") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Key geoms:
- `geom_point()` — scatter plots
- `geom_bar()` / `geom_col()` — bar charts
- `geom_line()` — line charts
- `geom_boxplot()` — box plots
- `geom_histogram()` — histograms

courses.title: Docker and Kubernetes
courses.description: Container orchestration with Docker and Kubernetes for scalable deployments.

lessons.title: Why Containers?
lessons.body:
Containers solve the 'it works on my machine' problem by packaging your app with all its dependencies.

**VMs vs Containers:**
- VMs include a full OS (heavy, slow to start)
- Containers share the host OS kernel (lightweight, fast)
- A container starts in milliseconds vs minutes for VMs

**Key benefits:**
- Consistency across environments
- Isolation between applications
- Easy scaling and deployment
- Efficient resource usage

Docker is the most popular container runtime. Let's install it and run our first container.

lessons.title: Docker Basics
lessons.body:
Essential Docker commands:

```bash
# Run a container
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx

# List containers
docker ps

# Build an image
docker build -t myapp .

# Stop/remove
docker stop <id>
docker rm <id>
```

**Dockerfile anatomy:**
```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Each instruction creates a layer. Layers are cached for faster rebuilds.

lessons.title: Docker Compose
lessons.body:
Docker Compose manages multi-container applications:

```yaml
version: '3.8'
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
```

Commands:
- `docker compose up` — Start all services
- `docker compose down` — Stop and remove
- `docker compose logs` — View logs
- `docker compose exec web sh` — Shell into container

courses.title: Flutter Mobile Development
courses.description: Build beautiful cross-platform mobile apps with Flutter and Dart.

lessons.title: Introduction to Flutter
lessons.body:
Flutter is Google's UI toolkit for building natively compiled applications for mobile, web, and desktop from a single codebase.

Why Flutter?
- Single codebase for iOS and Android
- Hot reload for instant development feedback
- Rich widget library
- Customizable with Material Design and Cupertino widgets
- Growing ecosystem and community

Setup: Install Flutter SDK, Android Studio or VS Code, and run `flutter doctor`.

lessons.title: Dart Language Essentials
lessons.body:
Dart is the language behind Flutter. Key features:

```dart
// Variables
var name = 'Alice';          // inferred type
String greeting = 'Hello';   // explicit type
final id = 42;               // runtime constant
const pi = 3.14;             // compile-time constant

// Null safety
String? nullableName;         // can be null
String nonNullName = 'Bob';   // cannot be null

// Functions
int add(int a, int b) => a + b;  // arrow syntax
```

Dart is strongly typed with sound null safety, making your code more reliable.

courses.title: Cybersecurity Basics
courses.description: Fundamentals of cybersecurity including network security, cryptography, and ethical hacking.

lessons.title: The Cybersecurity Landscape
lessons.body:
Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems, networks, and data from digital attacks.

**Common threats:**
- **Phishing**: Deceptive emails/messages to steal credentials
- **Malware**: Viruses, ransomware, spyware
- **Social Engineering**: Manipulating people into breaking security
- **DDoS**: Overwhelming systems with traffic
- **Zero-day**: Exploits for unknown vulnerabilities

**CIA Triad:**
- **Confidentiality**: Only authorized access
- **Integrity**: Data isn't tampered with
- **Availability**: Systems are accessible when needed

lessons.title: Network Security Fundamentals
lessons.body:
Understanding network security is essential for protecting data in transit.

**Key concepts:**
- **Firewalls**: Filter network traffic based on rules
- **VPN**: Encrypt traffic between endpoints
- **DNS Security**: Prevent DNS poisoning and hijacking
- **Network segmentation**: Isolate sensitive systems

**TCP/IP basics:**
- Three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK
- Ports: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 22 (SSH), 3306 (MySQL)
- OSI Model: Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Session → Presentation → Application

Tools: Wireshark for packet analysis, Nmap for port scanning.

lessons.title: Cryptography Essentials
lessons.body:
Cryptography is the foundation of information security.

**Symmetric encryption:**
- Same key to encrypt and decrypt
- Fast: AES-256, ChaCha20
- Key distribution is the challenge

**Asymmetric encryption:**
- Public/private key pair
- Slower: RSA, ECC
- Used for key exchange and digital signatures

**Hashing:**
- One-way transformation
- SHA-256, bcrypt for passwords
- Used for integrity verification

**TLS/SSL:**
- Combines asymmetric (key exchange) + symmetric (data transfer)
- HTTPS = HTTP + TLS
- Always use HTTPS for web traffic
